---
# On Walking Without Anywhere to Be

There is a particular kind of walk I have been taking for years now, and I have never once told anyone about it, because telling anyone about it would have required me to explain its purpose, and it has none. I leave the house without a destination. I turn left or right depending on some private weather in my body. I walk until I no longer feel like walking, and then I come home.

This is not exercise. This is not a commute. This is not a constitution around the park for the sake of the ten thousand steps some app has decided I should take. It is walking as its own activity, complete in itself, the way a poem is not a letter that failed to be practical. And I have come to believe that this purposeless movement is one of the few remaining things I do that has not been optimized, monetized, or converted into content.

---

The first thing you notice when you walk without anywhere to be is how much of your usual walking is a kind of violence. You are always cutting through the world. The street is an obstacle between you and the office, the grocery store, the gym. Trees are things you pass. People are things you pass. The light on the brick of a building at four in the afternoon in October is something you would have seen if you had been looking, which you were not, because you were thinking about the email you have to send, or the conversation you had this morning that you are now re-litigating in your head, adding the clever things you should have said, the patient things, the things that would have made you into a slightly better person than the one who actually opened her mouth.

But when you have nowhere to be, the email loosens its grip. Not immediately. The first twenty minutes of a purposeless walk are often just the same mental churn, the same loops, the same arguments with people who are not present. The mind is a donkey that has been driven hard for years, and it does not know how to stop just because the cart has been unhitched. It keeps pulling. It keeps leaning into the old yoke of productivity and self-improvement and relational anxiety. You have to let it tire itself out.

And then, somewhere around the second mile, or the third, something shifts. The churn quiets. And the world, which had been a blur of typography and pavement and other people's hurry, comes into focus with an almost painful clarity. You notice the way a magnolia bud has already formed its fuzzy casing for next spring, sitting on the branch like a small secret the tree is keeping. You notice that the sidewalk on the north side of Elm Street has been repaired in a patchwork of concrete decades, each square a slightly different shade of gray, so that walking it is like walking through a geological cross-section of the town's municipal history. You notice an old man watering his tomatoes at six in the evening, shirtless, with the unhurried competence of someone who has done this ten thousand times and will do it ten thousand more, and you feel a wave of something that is not quite envy and not quite love and not quite grief, but is related to all three.

This is attention. Not the attention that is demanded of us—the attention of notifications, of performance reviews, of the endless call to be present for this meeting or that crisis—but the attention that we give freely, that we spend the way a child spends, extravagantly and without accounting. William James wrote that the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will. He was right, but he was also describing something more like discipline than what I mean. What I mean is the opposite of discipline. What I mean is the attention that happens when you stop trying to attend, when you stop making attention into a task, and the world simply arrives.

---

I think about how much of my life has been spent in transit between destinations, and how little of it has been spent actually inhabiting the transit. The walk to school as a child was different. Children walk strangely, blessedly. They stop. They pick up sticks. They examine the flattened penny on the railroad track, the anthill, the interesting rock, the way the light comes through a leaf held up to the sun. They walk the way a river walks, which is to say they are not walking to get anywhere in particular, or if they are, they have entirely forgotten it in favor of the ditch full of tadpoles.

At some point we are cured of this. We are cured of it by adults who have somewhere to be, and who cannot understand why a child would want to stop and look at a mushroom growing out of a rotted stump when the car is right there and we are already late. We are cured of it by the internalized adult, the one who lives in our heads now and taps his foot and reminds us that we have things to do. We are cured of it by a culture that has converted every moment into an opportunity for self-betterment, so that even a walk must be a workout, even a meal must be optimized, even sleep must be tracked and scored, even rest must be productive rest, recovery, biohacking, investment in tomorrow's output.

I am not immune. I have counted my steps. I have listened to podcasts at 1.5 speed while walking through parks that deserved better of me. I have turned what should have been wandering into a demonstration of discipline, a thirty-minute brisk walk that lowered my resting heart rate and did nothing whatsoever for my soul.

But the purposeless walk has been slowly, quietly undoing some of that. It has been reminding me that I am an animal in a landscape, and that the landscape does not care about my goals, and that this not-caring is a tremendous relief. The oak tree is not trying to get anywhere. The hawk is not optimizing its afternoon. The rain does not have a five-year plan.

---

There is a Zen story about a man on a horse, and someone calls out to him, "Where are you going?" and the man says, "I don't know, ask the horse." I have thought about that story a great deal. The horse is momentum. The horse is the accumulated habits of a life, the defaults, the path of least resistance, the way we find ourselves halfway through another week without having decided to live it. Most of us are on that horse. Most of our institutions are that horse. The technological systems we have built are that horse, and they are very fast, and they do not know where they are going, and they have long since stopped listening to the man on their back, if he is still up there at all.

The purposeless walk is a way of getting off the horse. It is slow enough that you can actually feel your feet, which sounds simple and is in fact a revelation. Most of the time I have no sensation of my feet at all. They carry me around like a nervous pavilion and I never thank them. But on a walk with nowhere to be, I feel the heel strike, the roll through the arch, the push off the toe, the slight unevenness of my gait on the left side where I apparently favor one hip. I feel the ground through the soles of my shoes, or better, when I have remembered to take the shoes off in a grassy park, I feel it directly, the cool of the earth in the evening, the surprising give of moss.

This is not mindfulness as a wellness product. This is not a technique for reducing cortisol so that you can return to your desk a more efficient machine. This is just what happens when you give the body back to itself and the world back to the body. The mind, which has been squatting in the skull like a demanding tenant, finally pays a little rent. It notices things. It makes unexpected connections. Problems that seemed insoluble at the desk dissolve into a more generous perspective, not because you "solved" them but because you stopped gripping them so hard, and in the loosening they rearranged themselves into something more livable.

Some of my best thinking has happened when I was not trying to think. Some of my best decisions arrived on a Tuesday afternoon on a residential street with no architectural significance whatsoever, between a hedge and a fire hydrant, in the space of a single step.

---

I worry about what we are doing to our capacity for this. I worry about a generation growing up inside recommendation engines, for whom every moment of potential boredom—the waiting room, the elevator, the walk to the bus—is immediately filled, colonized, converted into content consumption. Boredom is the threshold. Boredom is the ugly, restless lobby you have to sit in before the elevator of genuine reverie arrives. If you never sit in the lobby, if you never endure the thirty seconds or three minutes of nothing-to-look-at, you never get on the elevator. You never rise into the floor of the mind where the strange and the useful and the beautiful reside.

The purposeless walk is a structured way of sitting in that lobby. It is a way of making boredom respectable again, of giving it a container so that we do not immediately reach for the phone. You are not "doing nothing" in a way that will make you feel like a failure. You are walking. Walking is a thing. It has a history. It has Thoreau and Wordsworth and Kant's daily circuit and Darwin's thinking path and the flâneurs and the pilgrims and every old man in every park in every city in the world who has earned the right to shuffle along a gravel path at a glacial pace, nodding at pigeons. You are in excellent company. You are performing an ancient human activity that requires no equipment, no subscription, and no explanation.

And yet I find I still hesitate to tell people about it. There is a shame attached to purposelessness in our culture that runs deep. To say "I went for a walk" is acceptable if you add "to clear my head" or "to get some exercise" or "to think through a problem." The walk must be instrumental. It must have a reason that can be justified to the internal auditor, that tap-tap-tapping clerk who follows us around with a clipboard, demanding to know the ROI of every hour.

The purposeless walk fires the auditor. Or rather, it does not fire him, but it stops answering his questions, and eventually he gets bored and wanders off, and then you are alone with the evening light and the magnolia buds and the old man and his tomatoes, and the clipboard is on the ground somewhere back at the last intersection, and you do not go back for it.

---

I have started to think of these walks as a kind of informal sabbath. Not the religious kind, with its rules and its dread of kindling fires, but something more casual and more private: a recurring release from the economy of usefulness. For the duration of the walk, I am not a worker, not a consumer, not a project, not a brand, not a node in a network. I am a mammal moving through a landscape at three miles an hour, which is the speed at which human beings have done almost all of their living for almost all of their history. Three miles an hour is the speed of conversation, of courtship, of tracking game, of fleeing slowly enough to survive, of carrying a child, of carrying water, of carrying news. Our bodies and our minds are shaped by that speed the way a riverbed is shaped by the water. When we go faster, we leave something behind. When we go slower, we pick something up.

What I pick up is hard to catalog. It is not information. It is more like a sediment of small perceptions that settles into the character and makes it, I hope, a little more permeable, a little more capable of being surprised. The person who has spent an hour looking at a heron standing in a drainage ditch, absolutely still, with the patience of something that has outlasted continents, is slightly different afterward. Not better, exactly. But more capacious. More able to hold contradiction and mess and the slow green persistence of things.

---

I do not want to make this sound like a prescription. The moment I turn this into advice—"take a purposeless walk! It will change your life!"—I have dragged it back onto the horse, I have given it a destination, I have handed it to the auditor for processing. The whole point is that it cannot be a technique. It can barely be a practice. It is closer to a permission. You are permitted to leave the house without a plan. You are permitted to turn down a street you have never turned down for no reason. You are permitted to stand on a corner and watch the light change from gold to rose to the particular lavender of a streetlight coming on, and to do this not because it will make you more creative or more productive or more resilient, but because it is what you feel like doing, and that is enough.

The enoughness of it is the hard part. We are trained from childhood to believe that we are not enough, that our hours are not enough, that every moment must be justified by its yield. The purposeless walk is a small heresy against that training. It is not going to topple any systems. It is not going to fix the world. But it might, for a mile or two, return you to yourself, and to the world, and to the ancient agreement between them that we made when we first stood up on two legs and started, for no reason other than curiosity, to walk.

I am going to go take one now. I do not know which direction. That is the whole point.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical personal essay turns an ordinary walk into a meditation on attention, purposelessness, and the pressure to optimize daily life.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate but composed, moving between personal confession and broad cultural critique. Its pathos lies in the speaker’s sense that attention and unmeasured time have been trained out of us, then partly recovered through small acts of noticing: magnolia buds, uneven sidewalk patches, tomatoes at dusk, the feel of a foot on the ground. The essay invites the reader not to adopt a new productivity ritual, but to grant themselves permission to wander without justification. Its recurring humor—the internal auditor, the horse of momentum—keeps the critique warm rather than scolding.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds purposeless walking as a refuge from optimization, consumption, and self-improvement culture. It gives unusual weight to ordinary sensory details and to boredom as a precondition for reverie. Its moral claim is that unproductive attention can be valuable in itself, not because it improves later performance but because it restores a person’s relation to the world.

## Evidence line
> The purposeless walk is a small heresy against that training.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive cluster of images—the horse, the auditor, the lobby of boredom—and repeatedly returns to the value of attention without instrumental purpose.
